concept.name: Rectangle pattern
concept.definition: A classical consolidation pattern in which price oscillates between a horizontal resistance line (at least two comparable highs) and a horizontal support line (at least two comparable lows), forming a trading range. It is directionally neutral: usually a continuation pause within the prevailing trend, but it can also mark significant tops and bottoms, and only the breakout assigns direction. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Bulls buy every dip to the same floor and bears sell every rally to the same ceiling; the range persists until one side runs out of ammunition and price escapes the box.
concept.mechanics: Draw parallel horizontal lines through at least two comparable highs and two comparable lows; ranges shorter than about three weeks are conventionally flags instead, while three-plus months is typical. Volume behavior is irregular (unlike triangles), but which direction attracts the most volume can hint at the resolution. Confirmation is a closing break of a boundary (optionally with a 3% price or 3-day filter and volume expansion); the broken boundary often flips polarity on a retest, and the target projects the rectangle's height from the breakout.
concept.formula: Price target = B +/- (R - S), where B = breakout price, R = resistance line, S = support line (sign follows breakout direction).
concept.failure_modes: False breakouts out of well-established ranges are notorious — the longer and more obvious the range, the more traders position for the break and the more rewarding a fake-out. Range-trading (buying support, selling resistance) also fails catastrophically on the final breakout that never returns.
concept.misconceptions: That a rectangle is bullish or bearish based on the prior trend — it is explicitly neutral until the break. Also that support/resistance lines must be touched at exactly equal prices; reasonably close touches suffice.
concept.example: After rallying to the low $40s, a stock churns between $30 and $40 for five months; a high-volume close above $40 projects a measured move of the $10 height toward $50, and broken $40 resistance later acts as support.

citations.source: Lo, Mamaysky & Wang, 'Foundations of Technical Analysis' (NBER Working Paper 7613)
